lead.text: *A field guide to the actual working trajectory of a modern professional life.*
Careers are not built by talent alone. They are built by a small number of decisions, executed well, over a long time. What follows is the practical playbook — not the inspirational one.

blocks.text: **THE IDEA — Your career is a portfolio of bets**

Every job is a bet on a specific combination of skills, relationships, market position, and personal growth. Most bets pay off modestly; a few pay off spectacularly; some go to zero.
The professional discipline is to make each bet with clear eyes about what you're betting on.
Not what you like. What you're actually good at, that others notice you're good at, that produces value in the world. Three overlapping circles:

items: What people are willing to pay for (value).

blocks.text: The intersection is where a durable career lives. Careers built on any two often stall.
**THE TOOL — The three-question strengths audit**

1. Where do people bring problems to me?
Which topics do colleagues, friends, or family consistently seek your opinion on? That signal is harder to fake than resume bullet points.
2. What comes easily to me that others struggle with?
Not what you'd wish you were good at. What is annoyingly easy for you and hard for smart people around you.
3. What do I still enjoy after a bad week?
The activities that survive bad moods and low energy are the ones with structural fit — not just situational enthusiasm.
Most people ask 'what should I do?' The better question is: 'what kind of problems do I want to spend the next decade solving?'
Then ask: where are those problems paid well? Where do they compound my abilities rather than plateau them? Where do they align with how I want my daily life to look?
**THE TOOL — A resume that actually works**

1. Impact over activity
'Managed a team of 8' is activity. 'Rebuilt onboarding process, reducing time-to-first-value from 21 days to 9' is impact. Every bullet should have a number, a before, or an after.
2. Verbs at the start
Led. Built. Shipped. Rebuilt. Reduced. Increased. Owned. Founded. Not 'responsible for.' Never 'helped with.'
3. Match the language
Read the job description. Use the specific terms they use. Not to game the ATS (though it helps) — because language mismatch reads as domain-mismatch to human readers too.
4. One page under 10 years, two under 20
Almost no career justifies more.
5. Update quarterly, not when needed
Update your CV every quarter with the last 90 days' wins. This is not for job-hunting; it is for you. It is the fastest way to notice you've stopped growing.
Interviews are not tests of your ability. They are tests of your ability to describe your ability. These are related, but different, skills.
**THE TOOL — The five interview stories**

Before any interview, prepare five stories from your career:
• A hard problem you solved.
• A time you failed and what you learned.
• A time you led without formal authority.
• A time you changed your mind after new evidence.
• A specific example of your best work.
For each: what was the situation, what you did, what was the impact, and what you'd do differently. Practice each out loud. Time each to 2 minutes.
You will not tell all five in one interview. You will be relieved that you have the right one ready when the specific question arrives.

The word 'networking' is offputting to almost everyone who is good at it. The people who are effective at professional relationships do not think of them as networking. They think of them as friendships that happen to include work.
**THE TOOL — A better model**

• Take an interest in people's actual work, not just what they can do for you.
• Send interesting things to interesting people, with no ask attached. Do this three times before you ever ask for anything.
• Follow up on introductions. If someone introduces you to someone, send them a note within a month saying what came of it.
• Say yes to inconvenient coffee meetings when you genuinely respect the person. Over years, this is the second-highest-ROI activity in a career.
• Highest is being the person people want to work with again. Which is not a networking skill — it is a work skill.

Your manager is the single most important professional relationship you have — for compensation, growth, assignments, and reputation. Managing that relationship actively is not sycophancy. It is basic professional practice.
**THE TOOL — Six moves that most people don't make**

1. In the first 30 days: 'What does success look like from your seat? What would make me easy to work with?' Then act on the answers.
2. Come to 1:1s with a written short list of what you're working on, blocked on, and need input on. Never come empty-handed.
3. Send a weekly 5-bullet update: what I shipped, what I'm working on, what I'm blocked on, decisions I need, feedback requested. Even if not asked for.
4. When they give feedback: thank them, do not defend, act on it, tell them what you changed. Compounds fast.
5. Do not surprise them. If something is going wrong, they should hear it from you first, before anyone else, ideally with your proposed fix.
6. Ask for feedback specifically: 'What's one thing I could do differently that would make my work easier for you to use?' The specific question produces actionable answers.
Doing good work is necessary. Being known for doing good work is also necessary. They are different projects.
**THE TOOL — Genuine visibility practices**

• Document your work. A shared doc, wiki, or team channel where your outputs live and can be found. Not to boast — so future colleagues can find your work when they need it.
• Give credit generously, publicly, specifically. 'This shipped because Priya did X and Sam did Y' — the person doing this is universally seen as more senior, not less.
• Present, teach, write. Internal or external. Even one lunch-and-learn per quarter compounds reputation.
• When someone asks how a project is going, have a one-sentence answer ready. Practice it. Say it cleanly.
• Never lie or inflate. The compounding downside of being caught doing this is worse than any short-term gain.
Money is not everything. But it is the medium in which much of your working life is denominated. Being deliberately underpaid is a form of self-harm.
**THE TOOL — Six moves for compensation**

1. Know your market. Sites like levels.fyi (tech), Glassdoor (broad), and industry-specific salary surveys give you a range. Use the range in conversations, not a single number.
2. Never name your number first if you can avoid it. If pushed: 'Based on my research on the market and my experience, I'm looking for something in the range of X to Y. Where does that fit for you?'
3. Negotiate every offer. Even a modest ask succeeds often, and the ceiling is not usually where the first offer lands.
4. Trade across compensation categories: base, bonus, equity, sign-on, benefits, PTO, remote flexibility. Flexibility often costs the employer less than base.
5. Revisit compensation on a schedule. Every 12–18 months of significant new responsibility justifies a conversation.
6. If your employer refuses to acknowledge market movements over 2+ years, the market itself is now your negotiating counter-party. Interview. Get offers. Decide with data.
Most career switches are less dramatic than they feel. You are not becoming a new person. You are recombining capabilities into a new role.
**THE TOOL — Three questions before you switch**

1. What skills of mine transfer directly — and what is the gap I need to close?
2. Who has already made this move, and can I spend 30 minutes with three of them?
3. What is the minimum viable version of this switch — a project, a side role, a class — that would tell me if I'll actually enjoy the new domain, before I commit fully?
Trial runs before commitments. It is astounding how many career switches happen without ever having spent a week in the new work.
Statistically, it will happen at least once. Sometimes twice. It is not evidence of failure. It is evidence of working long enough for anything unpredictable to happen at least once.
**THE TOOL — The first two weeks**

Week 1:
• Do not decide anything the first 48 hours.
• Review severance and benefits carefully. Consult a professional if anything is unclear.
• Update your CV using this playbook's rules.
• Write down a one-paragraph story: what happened, in your own words, in the way you'd tell a trusted friend. This is the narrative you'll use in future interviews.
• Reach out to 10–20 people who know you and your work. Don't hide. Most help comes from people who know you're looking.
Week 2:
• Have coffee (or Zoom) with three people from your list.
• Apply to roles that genuinely fit — not everything.
• Set a daily rhythm. Job-searching without structure produces low outputs and high anxiety.
• Take actual weekends. This is not a full-time hustle. It is a marathon.

Almost every knowledge worker's job is being reshaped by AI. Some jobs will disappear. Most will change. The distinction between people who thrive in the transition and people who don't is not technical skill — it is willingness to redesign their own work.
**THE TOOL — Three moves for AI-era resilience**

1. Use AI daily in your current role. Not theoretically. Daily. Discover what it changes about your work.
2. Move up the abstraction ladder. AI is best at execution of well-specified tasks. Your value grows in problem-definition, judgment, and cross-functional synthesis — exactly what earlier Levels of this book trained.
3. Build public artifacts. Write. Publish. Speak. Reputation portable across companies matters more in a fast-changing economy than tenure within any single one.
**THE GREAT MINDS COUNCIL — On the career, from the Council**

Through Peter Drucker's lens:
'The most important thing in communication is hearing what isn't said.' A career is often built by noticing what your manager hasn't asked for but needs.
Through Andy Grove's lens:
'Your career is your business.' You are its CEO. Treat it with the same seriousness.
Through Warren Buffett's lens:
'You only have to do a very few things right in your life so long as you don't do too many things wrong.' Careers are built by not making career-killing mistakes, not by making genius moves.
Through Naval Ravikant's lens:
'Play long-term games with long-term people.' Reputation compounds across decades.
Through Cal Newport's lens:
'Be so good they can't ignore you.' Skill development is the most reliable career strategy.
Where the Council might be wrong:
Career optimization can consume the life it was meant to fund. Do not build a career at the price of the health, relationships, and character that make a career worth having.
REMEMBER THIS
*“Your career is a portfolio of bets. Make each one with clear eyes.”*
